look_here_first: Flip the leaf first. Mustang grape has a dense white-to-rusty woolly tomentum on the lower surface that essentially hides the blade surface and veins. Then confirm broad heart- to kidney-shaped leaves and large dark berries usually 12 mm or more.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: vigorous high-climbing woody vine with shredding bark

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: young branchlets densely to sparsely tomentose

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: leaves broad cordate to nearly reniform, usually unlobed or shallowly lobed but sometimes deeply 3–5-lobed on vigorous shoots

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: leaf underside densely white to rusty tomentose, surface largely concealed by hairs

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: upper leaf surface becomes green and much less hairy

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: tendrils or inflorescences occur opposite leaves and at only two consecutive nodes

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: berries usually black or dark red, slightly or not glaucous, commonly 12+ mm

lookalikes.differences: Vitis berlandieri: Lower leaf surface is visible and only sparsely hairy to nearly glabrous in V. berlandieri; its fruit is more strongly glaucous and clusters are shorter/compact. Vitis cinerea: V. cinerea has a visible gray/green lower leaf surface with webby and short hairs rather than the solid white felt of V. mustangensis, and its berries are much smaller. Vitis palmata: V. palmata has uniformly red/purplish branchlets and usually deeply lobed glabrous leaves, not a white-felted underside.
